old: Its extra syllable didn't come from meaning — it came from someone mishearing where a French article ended and a noun began.
The French phrase for 'the war supplies' got glued together the wrong way, and English kept the mistake.
It's really just munition with a stray article stuck to its front.
clues: This military noun for a kind of supply was born from a slip of the ear, when French speakers misheard the word for 'the' as part of the word itself.
It means the bullets, shells and cartridges that guns fire, not the weapons themselves. That accidental extra syllable stuck and became the standard English word.
In a debate, a damaging fact you hand your opponent is called this. It shares a Latin root with a shorter sibling word that never picked up the mistaken article.
